utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, did I understand you to say yesterday that your principal motive for joining the police was in order that you could obtain a firearm?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was that, on your judgement, the approach of many of those who were in the military police, that they wanted to be armed?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was of all of us down there, to defend ourselves, because the Serbs had already started the war. We, who had no weapons, naturally wanted to have weapons in order to protect ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. We heard of various people not being members of the military police, apparently not being members of any armed unit, but nevertheless having hunting rifles and operating as village guards. You weren't prepared to do your duty at that level; you wanted to be a member of a unit, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to have a weapon in order to protect my family, because I was not a hunter so I didn't have even a hunting rifle. Therefore, I had to look, to see, some way to take care of myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You tell us that when you were working together with Muslims, somebody said something about an Islamic state, a Djamahirija. Who was it who said that, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't one who said that, many said that. It was already, how shall I put it, it was a habit of theirs to pull our leg for a number of years, and that is how they greeted us, like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Pulling your leg is one thing; saying something seriously is another. You didn't use the phrase "pulling our leg" or your leg yesterday, but is that all it was, a sort of joke?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Afterwards, it happened every day. For instance, on one occasion, a colleague who was with me told me to look at the sky. We were doing the third shift between the municipality of Vitez and the municipality of Busovaca. He said, "Tomic, look up. What do I see?" And what do I see? I see the moon and the stars. And he told me, "Well, when you see up there the chequerboard, that is when you will have living space here. As long as there are stars and a moon up there, we shall be ruling here." That is what he told me, and he really meant it, and warned me to mind that we never find one another -- one opposite the other when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us the name of this person? You see, if you're suggesting these were serious observations, I'd like the names of the people who made them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the name. But he now works for the civilian police in Vitez together with Croats. I know that he comes from Sivrino Selo. I can't remember his name.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. When was all this happening, Mr. Tomic, in the autumn of 1992 - have I got the picture right? - or was it earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Autumn of 1992.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before your injury in November, how long had you been an active member of the military police, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You'd had your training, hadn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, month-long. And after that month I was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying that you were a reserve policeman or a full-time, active policeman?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a member of the military police at the time when I was injured, and at that time we were already accommodated in what you could call the barracks in Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you. I've got two very short passages from a large exhibit called 511, and I've already flagged them. So if the usher would be good enough. The English version has got -- sorry, I didn't tag them. The document that's coming your way is a record of work of the military police in 1992, and I only want your comment on two passages of it. It's the green tags for him and it's the green tags for us. I think this is page 12, for reference purposes, in the English. This record of the work of the military police from 1992 says this, and this is a short paragraph, you'll find, beside the green tag: "Military police units include battalions, companies, and platoons which, in accordance with the territorial principle, cover individual zones of operations. "The First Battalion of the Military Police, formed exclusively from active officers, has three companies: the First Company based in Vitez ..." and then it deals with the second and third, and it goes on to say, "The personnel of this battalion are trained for the most difficult and most important military police tasks." Do you agree with that assessment of what you were doing in 1992, please, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In what way do you say that this description is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because my primary task -- I was with the traffic platoon, and my task was to look after the traffic of goods and people, because at that time humanitarian relief, that is, food supplies and medicines, were arriving from the Republic of Croatia, and who knows from what other parts. Our task, the task of our platoon, was simply to provide security for the free transport of goods, of people, and this humanitarian relief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you must have had some idea of what other platoons of the 1st Company of military police were doing in Vitez. Does this description of their work fit with your understanding of what they were doing, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No idea of what the rest of the military police were doing; is that really what you're telling us, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only make guesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's look at the next and second tag. If you go to the second green marker on the papers that you have, Mr. Tomic, and we're on page 13, this paragraph deals with training and it says: "Faced with the problem of professional training and personnel selection, efforts were made to ensure permanent training for members of the military police force at a training centre. A curriculum was drawn up in cooperation with professional bodies of the MUP RH/the Interior Ministry of the Republic of Croatia/. On 20 September 1992 the Military Police Training Centre was founded in Neum. The conduct of professional training was entrusted to instructors from the Interior Ministry of the Republic of Croatia. Since its foundation, about 300 members of the military police force have received training there. All participants who complete the training course successfully are sent to the active units of the military police, where they are proving themselves to be the foundation of the military police force by the quality of their work." Well, now you had this month's training, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The description here, no doubt, fits with your recollection. You were being trained by instructors from Croatia; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, who were you being trained by?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Well, who were you being trained by, if not by instructors from Croatia? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were from Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you give us any of their names?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot really recall the names, but I know they were Herzegovinians --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a document --

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- that they were not from the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This is not a document prepared by anybody except the military police themselves. Can you explain how it could be suggested that the Republic of Croatia was training you when in fact you were being trained by somebody else, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think that's probably a comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe, Your Honour, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's take that document back, then, please, and see if you can help us with some other things about the military police. Pasko Ljubicic was the commander, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But let's not trouble ourselves for the time being with the people at the top. Let's trouble ourselves with the people at your level. No doubt in your months there you met some people you already knew and you made some new contacts and new friends. Would that be about right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, tell us: Who were your friends, please, in the military police when you were working in the autumn of 1992?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were six, seven. Depends on how many of us were in the department. And yes, we kept each other's company, because we served on the same shifts and we were together --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Their names, please, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, for instance, Dusko Prusac from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Glavas, Mladen Glavas - I think his first name is Mladen - from Busovaca again. Srecko -- I can't remember his surname. He comes from Dusina, from Lasva, towards Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Another one? Another name?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was Franjo Ramljak, from Zenica; Tikvic, from Zenica again.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That will do for the time being. Did any of these people get killed in the fighting or did they all survive?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These people were with me that night when we were stopped in Kruscica, and I think -- I'm not seeing them. That is, I'm still seeing the two who live in Vitez. The other ones I don't know. But I've been seeing Franjo Ramljak and this one, Tikvic, from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let's now go back to the top level of the military police and also to its organisation. Tell us, please, about the Jokers. That's part of the military police. Just tell us about them.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot tell you anything about it, because I do not know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You know the name. It was part of the military police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've heard about it, but to know something, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was in the Jokers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many military police all together were there, so that we've got some picture of this body that you were a member of? How many?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think some 120, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. And the Jokers were a part of that 120, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. So not a very large body, Mr. Tomic. Think back, please. Can you not give us any idea when the word "Jokers" was first used or who was in the Jokers? Try and help us, please.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot help you, because I was -- because I was at home. And about all those events in the early days in the war, I knew nothing, and after that. And even if somebody knew something about it, he was rather reluctant to talk about that because --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm going to come back to that a little later. Can we just look at two documents now that deal with the attack you suffered. You no doubt got to discover, either at the time or afterwards, that you were attacked because there had been a Croat murder of Muslims on the previous day. Did you discover that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We knew nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you subsequently discover that that was the reason, or the probable reason, for the attack on you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard that there had been an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is dealt in the evidence of Nihad Rebihic at page 8342. Just two documents of record that cover the incident. First 287.5. The original for the witness, please, English on the ELMO, first page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This, Mr. Tomic, is a document, and you can see that it's signed by Ljubicic. It's dated the 20th of November, it goes to the Mostar Ministry of Defence, and it sets out how, at about 1.20 on the 20th of November, on the road between Vitez and Kruscica, members of the BH army halted an official vehicle of the active duty returning from its regular shift, a vehicle occupied by -- and six names are set out, including yours. Before we pass on, which are the two names are the people to whom you still speak, please? Numbers?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5, Vinko Tikvic; and 6, Franjo Ramljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It goes on to say: "After their vehicle was halted the, said military policemen were disarmed and taken to the army premises in Kruscica. Dragan Botic, a cook in our unit, was with the military policemen." And it then goes on, on the next sheet in the English, but it's on the same page for you, Mr. Tomic, to say: "At 1.30, the commander of the Vitez active-duty VP phoned, Sefkija Dzidic, the commander of the Vitez BH army, demanding an immediate release of the apprehended military policeman. Sefkija Dzidic said there would be no problems, that his men acted out of rage at the murder which had occurred the previous night, and that our men would suffer no harm. "Immediately after this telephone conversation, the commander of the active-duty VP called Major General Slobodan Praljak and informed him about the incident. After this, contact was made every 15 minutes with Travnik HVO headquarters. Present there were the said Major General, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Colonel Blaskic, and Mr. Dario Kordic, the president of the HZ HB, who did not allow the launching of an operation for the release of our men." Pausing there, did you discover anything about why a Croatian general was present at the time and involved in this business, please, Mr. Tomic?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't the least idea what was going on outside the garage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you ever discover -- you must have been concerned with what happened when you regained consciousness and learnt about events. Did you ever discover why it was that Mr. Kordic had not allowed an operation to release you?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, let me just object to this document on the ground that the document itself is not signed and the Prosecution has not laid an appropriate foundation for the admissibility of this document, as is their obligation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We've dealt with this sort of objection before and made the comment that documents speak for themselves. The fact that there is no signature, although there is a written name at the bottom -- we can see the commander of the battalion, Ljubicic, appears. Normally we have treated such documents as admissible but to decide what weight to give them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We'll admit the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: My question was: Did you ever discover, after you regained consciousness, why it was that Dario Kordic had not allowed a launching of an operation for your release?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I haven't the slightest what was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. I only want you to look at the rest of the document - it won't take long - for your comments on its accuracy so far as you can judge it. "At about 6.45, the apprehended policeman, the cook, and the civilian named Rajic, a mere passerby, arrived at the premises of the active-duty VP in Vitez. All of them were in a bad medical condition, owing to the injuries they received from the members of the Kruscica BH army. Four policemen were urgently taken to the Travnik hospital because they had received life-threatening injuries. Subsequently, the rest of the policemen were taken to the same hospital. "We have videotaped the injuries received by the four policemen and have a videotape showing these. It presents a classic example of barbarism because our men were butchered. They were stabbed. They had their," -- and it's not clear -- something cut, "and HVO letters incised into various parts of their bodies." Just pausing there, does that accord with your recollection or information as to what happened to you and your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there were these things, but it's not all accurate. I don't know. I remembered until the second treatment, as we used to call it, when I was hit with the butt of a machine-gun, and when I sustained those fractures and then fainted. I don't know when. And I woke up -- I came to in Nova Bila.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we'll just see what's said about that. The last few lines say this: "Medical records reveal that all the injured received severe bodily injuries. "Two military policemen were sent home for home care, four were retained at the Nova Bila hospital for treatment, and one - Dragan Tomic - was urgently sent to the hospital in Split because he was in a very bad condition. "As a result of an incident, tension increased primarily among the men in our unit, but also among the other HVO members, both in Vitez and in Busovaca." Now, insofar as it describes your medical movements and treatment, that would appear to be accurate; right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One other short document to look at on the same topic, 289.2. Now, this is a document; I don't suggest you will have seen this. It's the following day and comes from Valentin Coric. Can you just explain who he was, if you know? If you don't know, say so.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know anything about this document. It's the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you know the name of the person who signed it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name of the person. He was known through the media.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What was his job?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was, I think, the Minister of Foreign Affairs, or something to that effect, in Bosnia-Herzegovina. But I can't be sure exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, this document, just quickly read it, goes to the 1st Active-Duty Military Police Company in Vitez, informed of their report, which is the last document we've looked at, it goes on to say: "Prevent acts of retribution from our soldiers because they might lead to new clashes between Muslims and Croats which could have unforeseeable consequences. Take measures against the perpetrators of last night's murder of Muslims if they are HVO soldiers (you have not reported on this so please do it). We will take measures against BH army soldiers through their command." Were you aware, after the event, when you regained consciousness, were you aware of murder or murders of Muslims at about the time that you were injured and associated with your injuries?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in hospital I didn't even know what my own name was. I couldn't eat; I didn't eat for about a fortnight. I didn't care about anything at all. And I saw my wife and my children through a kind of mist --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, I understand all that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew nothing about documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The question I'm asking you is: Did you discover subsequently, when you had recovered to the extent that you did, did you discover subsequently that there had been killings, or a killing, of Muslims all connected with the attack on you, please?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but various rumours were going around. Some were true; others were not. I have three sons, I had two at the time, and I did not want to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. lay any emphasis on this because we live in a mixed neighbourhood. I have Muslim neighbours; in my hamlet there are Muslims. If somebody did something to me, I would deal with it myself. I didn't need help from anyone. I would go and talk to that person or not, as the case may be. I am not an investigator, and if I did see something, I don't know what I would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: All right. Only a couple more topics I want to raise with you very briefly. When you came out of hospital, I think you reported twice to the military police to try and join up again, and you were rejected; is that about right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reported because that's what I was supposed to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did this keep you in contact with your colleagues at the police, including Vinko Tikvic and Franjo Ramljak? Did that keep you in contact with them?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, of course, on the 16th of April you just were woken up by the detonations, and you tell us you went straight to Lazine; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you can't tell us anything from your own observations of what actually happened on the 16th of April at Ahmici, can you?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. That's your evidence. As a matter of fact, did you take a rifle with you when you went to Lazine?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Was it your police rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So although you were not working for the police, you were allowed to keep your rifle at home; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At my insistence, the rifle stayed with me because of all these events. So I did have one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who gave you permission to keep this rifle?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case nobody even asked me, but I simply -- I had received it and so I kept it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did all the military policemen take their rifles home? Were there enough rifles for the military police to do that?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a rifle that was issued to me. I was issued with it; it was mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. You say that you stayed in Lazine until when?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, until the end of September. Toward the end of September.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What's the name of your father?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Franjo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your area, as we know from the map, is all very close to Dubravica, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can we have private session just for a minute to identify someone by name?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The person whose name I've just provided you left the area of Donja Dubravica in June of 1993, before you had returned to the military police. Do you remember his departure? Just yes or no, not naming the person.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, it's right, isn't it, that he signed a document as a result of which much of his property passed to other people, including to you, and he left the area with little more than his lorry?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He has now come back, we are neighbours again, and he has everything. He speaks well of us. And I wasn't there when he left, but we did come across each other while these unhappy events were going on, we did meet occasionally. For his property to be preserved, he gave it to people. He drew up some kind of contract.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Whatever may have happened since, Mr. Tomic, the contract that he drew up whereby property passed to you and to others was something that was done under pressure, wasn't it, at the time?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Even though you were in Lazine, as you say, defending that village, you were well able to take part in the cleansing of the area of people like the man I've just referred to, and whose name we aren't using.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not correct. I wasn't in the trench all the time. I did go home occasionally.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Last topic: You eventually joined the police again in October of 1993.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As we know, you would have kept up with, and were now able to talk to people like Vinko Tikvic and Franjo Ramljak; yes?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: By now, no one in your valley can have been ignorant, I suggest to you, of the attack on Ahmici; you would accept that, wouldn't you? Everybody knew about that attack.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a tragedy that people are reluctant to talk about.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They may be reluctant, Mr. Tomic, but let's deal with it in stages. You knew by the time you rejoined the military police that there had been an HVO attack on and massacre at Ahmici; correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew, but from rumours that it had happened. And of course whoever did that should be held responsible for it, for that tragedy.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, you're a military policeman who, on your evidence, was unavoidably detained elsewhere on the night of the 15th/16th. But from your evidence, Vinko Tikvic and Franjo Ramljak, among others, are military policemen who are alive and well and who were working on that night; would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, when you rejoined the military police, Mr. Tomic, did you never ask them what they'd done on that night or what had happened?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You never once, of any one of the military police, you never asked them what had happened, what Ljubicic had done, or how it had gone wrong?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I never asked anyone about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Your Honour, just a few questions for clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tomic, at the beginning of your examination it was suggested to you that you joined the military police in order to obtain a weapon; you remember this, the Prosecutor said that.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I joined the civilian police for that reason, to get a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: To clarify things, after you were rejected or, rather, after you did not manage to join the army in Croatia to fight against the JNA, you joined the reserve police force in Vitez; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long were you part of the reserve civilian police force in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Less than a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that you joined the military police.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were in Neum for your training.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You said that this is a town in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: We are talking about September 1992. Who, at that time, was the only enemy of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs, the Serbian army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were shown a document which is, in fact, a report about your beating and the beating up of your colleagues in Fatina Vodica by members of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. On that occasion were you ever contacted by any organs of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina for the perpetrators to be established, or were you ever contacted by representatives of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: A unit was mentioned called the Jokers, and you said you didn't know much about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For Their Honours, I would like to draw attention to the fact that Witness AS testified that that unit was established in late January or early February 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time you were on sick-leave; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The man whose name we will not mention was referred to, and he drew up a contract transferring his property to his fellow villagers. Has he come back to the village?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Has all his property been restored to him?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Is he grateful to his fellow villagers for this?

utterances.speaker: DRAGAN TOMIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tomic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, which is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Our next witness is Mr. Marijan Strukar. Your Honour, before the witness comes in, just a brief explanation and a request. Marijan Strukar arrived in The Hague last night. He brought three short documents with him which are relevant for this case, and I would like to tender them into evidence. Of course they have not been translated, unfortunately, but the text is very brief so I suggest we put these three short documents on the ELMO. I have given copies to the interpreters' booths, and they can be translated very soon and entered into the evidence, if you will permit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What are the documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: These are two summons to join the civilian protection, and one certificate belonging to the Vitez Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strukar, good morning. On behalf of the Defence of Mr. Mario Cerkez I will conduct your examination. Please try to recall the events to the best of your ability; we all know that a lot of time has elapsed since 1993. Also please bear in mind that you should speak slowly and pause before giving your replies so that the interpreters can do their job. Mr. Strukar, for the record, would you please tell us your full name and date and place of your birth?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My name is Marijan Strukar. I was born on the 6th of May, 1956, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Do you live in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in Travnik but I live in Vitez. There was no hospital in Vitez so that's why I was born in Travnik. But I've been living in Vitez all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you would consider yourself a native of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: By nationality, you're a Croat, a Roman Catholic.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You completed secondary school of engineering in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, engineering.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're an engineering technician by profession, and today you are employed in an insurance company called Euroherc.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're head of the branch office in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're married and a father of two children.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have two sisters and a brother.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you serve in the former JNA?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you acquire any rank after your military service?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a rank exactly. I was a private, a private First Class. You became a private First Class after completing a course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So that was the lowest rank in the then-hierarchy?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. You couldn't consider it a proper rank.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Since 19 -- from 1987 until the outbreak of the war you were employed; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You worked in Vitezit as head of the plant maintenance service and later as the head of production; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the ethnic make-up of the employees in the Vitezit company where you worked?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you that no one actually thought about it at the time. The ethnic make-up reflected the general ethnic make-up of Vitez. I can't say whether there were more Croats or Muslims or Serbs, but Vitezit reflected the whole population of Vitez, because it was the biggest factory in Vitez. It employed 3.000 workers, and they were of all ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Apart from your regular job, you were also active in another field. Would you tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, my father was a volunteer firefighter, and quite early on he got me to join the volunteer fire brigade. So when the war broke out, I had been a member for 21 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And your long years of service, did it result in a formal post in the volunteer fire brigade?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, it was not a professional unit. We were not paid. We simply acquired experience. And for the last seven years before the war, I was the leader of a unit of the volunteer fire brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you have a superior, so to say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I don't know if you understand what I mean by "leader of a unit." That's an operative leader who leads the men when putting out a fire. But there are 24 hours in the day, and the fire-fighting can go on for a hour or two. But there was also a president and a secretary of the association, and they were in charge when there was no fire to be put out, when there was just administrative work to be done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you were a firefighter in the field, so to say?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the president. Who was the president of the association?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, we had to elect him from time to time. That's how it was. And it changed every year. I don't know if I can remember who it was at the time or who it was every time, but it was then someone who had the same last name as me. His last name was also Strukar, but I don't know if we are related or not. He may be a distant relative. His name is Anto. And the other one, who was more important, in our view, was called Sead Smriko. The president was there just to sign papers and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the man you considered to be the most important man was Sead Smriko in your organisation?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Smriko is a Muslim by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And for a time, you were also active in the conference of the youth association of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, for a time. I was even chairman of the municipal conference of the youth association for a year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, tell us, please, where the house belonging to your parents where you grew up was located in Vitez. Where was it situated?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, if you look at the town centre proper and if you move towards the suburbs of Vitez, you would come to the family houses. And my particular house was in that area, north-west of the centre of town, that is to say, moving towards Travnik and the Catholic church, which is about a kilometre away from the centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Later on, you built your own house near your parents' house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Some ten metres away from my parents' house, actually. I had a small property there and got all the papers I needed to construct my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You described the position of your house and said it was near the Catholic church, but the church was near a part of Vitez running along the Lasva River. What name does that area go by?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You're asking me what it was called? We referred to it, the locals called it -- that is to say, us local inhabitants called it Mahala; and more recently, that is to say, during the war and after the war, many -- and maybe people -- many people think that this is Stari Vitez, old Vitez. But those of us who have lived there for many years know that that was never referred to as Stari Vitez before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the section you're talking about is the Mahala, which was almost exclusively inhabited by Muslims; is that right? There were some Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Croats, but mostly Muslims; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So for as long as you can remember, you and all the inhabitants of Vitez called that the Mahala; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But during the war people began to refer to it as Stari Vitez, old Vitez, which today seems to have become synonymous for the area that was actually originally referred to as Mahala; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But you say that is incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's right, because the people who were born and bred in Vitez, the old inhabitants of Vitez, know that Vitez was formed from a part that belonged to Austro-Hungary. And there was the Han company. And this was the old Vitez which is in all the maps and ancient manuscripts and charters, and that section was always known and called Mahala. But during the war, on the radio, we used to hear that the code for the Muslim army, when referring to Mahala, that it was referred to as Stari Grad, Stari Vitez, old town or old Vitez. And it was interesting for us to hear on the news that it was -- that Stari Vitez was being attacked. We knew that in fact this was Mahala, because you would otherwise think that it was -- that the town had developed from that old part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understand you correctly, you -- Stari Vitez was the part that stretched from the old train station; that's Stari Vitez today as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But compared to Mahala, how far is that part of town?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I would say it was three kilometres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So they have nothing in common, no points in common?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps that makes it clearer. Mr. Strukar, were you given any military assignments or were you members -- were you a member of military units of any kind until the conflict broke out in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, no, not military units. I said that I was a member of the volunteer fire prevention unit. I don't really consider that a unit of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, your voluntary fire prevention unit came under the civil defence department, did it not?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Where was the fire brigade itself located?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: If you understood me when I explained to you where my own house was located, then you would go towards the centre of Vitez and some two to three hundred metres below my house, in the part called Mahala that I just spoke about a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So the fire brigade building with the vehicles and equipment was located in the part of town named Mahala; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I asked you at the beginning about the national composition of the employees of the company you worked for, Vitezit, and you said that that reflected the composition of the population in the area, in Vitez. Now I'm going to ask you what the national composition of the volunteer fire prevention society was where you worked.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Let me say again, at that time that was not important. We didn't think about things like that or discuss them. However, when a counting of heads started, so to speak, it was interesting to note -- and let me repeat again: The volunteer fire prevention society were people who liked the job. They were not paid for it. And the unit was built up according to how much each of us had contributed to fire prevention. And in 1992, that -- the basic unit, without the young ones, the young firemen, it had about 19, 20 Croats and 5 or 6 Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you went to put out fires in 1992 and later on in 1993, when you were called up, were you thinking about whether you were going to extinguish a fire in a Muslim house or Croatian house, or did you ever think about things like that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, did your volunteer fire prevention unit in October 1992 go to Ahmici to extinguish any fires or do anything there?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Ahmici. Well, there were interventions everywhere, daily, on a daily basis that last year. And when I say "that last year," I mean the end -- after the war ended in Slovenia, and so on. And in that particular war of ours, there were a number of interventions, and I assume that you are thinking about the events that accompanied the first conflict at that time. The BH army, in fact, the Muslim army. I assume you mean that, between the BH army and the HVO. I'm sure you mean that particular incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we speed this up a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will try, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Strukar, I do have that event in mind, at the barricade, the Catholic cemetery, and the village of Ahmici. The Chamber heard that some houses were set fire to on that occasion. Did your unit intervene?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, we intervened. We got down to the village. But there were still bullets flying. I wasn't a fighter. Perhaps the bullets were high up and flying through the trees. But they said, "There's nothing for you to look for here. Get back." So we came to Ahmici, but we didn't put any fires out. We just returned, went back.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So at that time -- and we're talking about the second half of 1992. We have heard testimony about that in the town of Vitez there were numerous incidents, explosions. Bombs were thrown, grenades, and so on, and I'm sure that you were called out, your fire prevention unit was called out. Can you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, usually when something happens, explodes somewhere, it usually happened at night, and we didn't know what had actually happened. And as soon as there was an explosion of any kind, this would be accompanied by fire, by burning, and people from the neighbouring houses would call out the fire brigade straight away and the fire brigade would go out to put out the fire, and we extinguished all the fires that were burning. If they had gone out themselves, we wouldn't have to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But as you were born and bred in Vitez, I'm sure you know the owners of the premises that you were called out to extinguish fires. Were they just Muslim properties and premises or Croatian ones as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I can't say that they were exclusively one or the other. There were many premises, many buildings, and the owners, the proprietors, were of all nationalities. Sometimes we didn't know even who they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Strukar, we have heard about two characteristic explosions that were planted in the Borovo shop and the Privredna Banka premises, explosive devices planted there. Can you tell us whether you intervened, whether you were called out in those two cases?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I'd have to differentiate and separate the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you give us a yes/no answer, please?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We went to the bank, yes, but we didn't go to the Borovo shop, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Strukar, the explosion in the Borovo shop, you learnt about that -- the fact -- you learnt about what had actually happened later on. Could you briefly, for purposes of illustration, tell us what you learnt? Who threw the bomb in the Borovo shop, and why?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Let me just say that that Borovo shop was bombed on the night when Jajce fell and when many refugees fled from Jajce to Vitez. It was raining. It was a terrible site. The children were wet. Us firemen were the only organised people who were able to help those people, so we put the children up in the nursery school, in the sports hall, and that's when the explosion was heard. And that was terrible for me to hear, because I thought: What madman, what idiot, could have done that in this kind of situation? And sometimes I was on duty with a young man who was from Zenica. I have to say that. And later on I heard that some of these -- that it was some young men from Cajdras who did this. And I asked them, "Did you actually do that?" And they said, "Yes." And I said, "Why?" "Well, we found Tito's picture, photograph, on the wall and we decided to blow the shop up." So they just threw in this bomb, this grenade, into the shop to blow up Tito's picture which they saw on the wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Strukar, when you went to the Privredna Banka Travnik premises, something unusual had happened there. Could you briefly tell us what that was?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, let me say, before I go into an explanation, that the position of the -- that is to say, my position, because I was the commander, the leader, of that fire brigade unit, the position where my fire brigade was located and where the Muslim police was located, we were next door to each other. There was just one wall between our fire brigade and the police department. And I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you speak a little slower, please. I think that everybody is finding it difficult to follow.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I'll try. So we were next door to each other, and there were no problems up until then. I was at the time next to the fire brigade building. And there was a regular shift, three members, they were on duty and they were expecting a fire which was -- and Suljeman Kalco, Sejo, phoned. The telephone rang, he phoned up, and they said, "Marijan's here." He asked to speak to me and he said, "Hurry up. It's the bank." That means that the bank was on fire, and his apartment was above the bank. So I took a driver with me and another man who was on duty, and it took us one minute to take the truck and the water and to reach the bank building. The siren was going full blast. We wanted to collect all the firefighters, and I told them that when they had all gathered, that they were to be sent to the bank building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you intervened when Mr. Smriko called you up. It took you one minute to get there. You told your colleagues in the fire brigade that they should follow you and come and help you out.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, when they were able to round them up from their homes, three or four minutes later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you got to the scene very quickly.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. We were wearing pyjamas. It was about 9.00 in the -- that is, my helper was wearing pyjamas. He came to help me out. It was about 9.00 and the building was on fire. We started putting out the fire. I tried to reach my deputy on my cell phone, because I was afraid that the whole building would explode. So I called my deputy and he said, "Marijan, do what you can on your own. We won't be able to help you out."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you asked for reinforcements and another fire engine because you were afraid that the fire would spread. But via radio communication you were told from the officer on duty that you were to put the fire out yourself, that nobody could come and help you; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You put the fire out, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that you went back to the fire brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I suppose you wanted to know why you were not reinforced.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. I was angry that nobody had come to help us, and I started shouting as soon as I left the fire engine. But they were all sitting down. When a team comes back, they would prepare and stock up again so that if a fire broke out, you would get things ready to go out and put another fire out. But they were all sitting down in the garage next to the vehicles, next to the fire engine, and I said, "Well, what's happening?" They said, "Well, we're under arrest. We've been taken into custody." We asked who and they said, "The police." And I was very angry. I went to the police station and the policemen to see what was going on, and they were surprised to see me. They said, "What are you doing there?" and I said, "Well, the bank was on fire." They said, "Well, where did you come out from?" and I said, well, we'd come out of the fire brigade. They couldn't understand that we had done all this so quickly, and they began to apologise. But I never actually learnt the real reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you went to put out the fire at the bank, you were told that the other team didn't turn up because the firemen had been taken prisoner by the Muslim police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you given an explanation as to why the Muslim police had reacted in that fashion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Never officially. We never received an official explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And informally, unofficially?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, people talked about it - because I was interested in learning the real reason - and people talked about it, although I found the explanation a little funny. They said that somebody had told them that we would think up a fire just to be able to steal a fire engine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We said at the beginning, Mr. Strukar, that your fire prevention activity came under the department of civil defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's right, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have brought two documents with you, two originals. I should like to ask you now -- we're going to place them on the ELMO for everybody to be able to see, and we'd like to ask the interpreters to translate them for us. And then I'd like to hear your comments.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters kindly request that counsel read out the document as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, you are asked to read out the document by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This document will be numbered D119/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, on the screen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not an objection, Mr. President. I'm trying to help the Chamber. We do have the translation for these documents. We have them translated for a very simple reason: They were used in another case previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you have the translation, let's have them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That's the other document. Yes, that's the first one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got the translation? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, this is a summons sent to you by Strbac, Dragan, Dragan Strbac, and we heard that he was in charge of civil defence matters in the municipality. The summons was sent to you on the 23rd of November, 1992, which you can see in the upper left-hand corner. It is "The Croatian Defence Council of Vitez," the heading. You are being summoned to join the fire prevention unit and the Vitez fire brigade on the 23rd of November; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This same summons, that same day, you received from another organ.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to ask the usher to help us out and distribute that document. [In English] The English translation on the ELMO and the original to the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Defence Exhibit D120/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This second document is a summons again to report to the civil defence department, the fire brigade of Vitez, on that same day, the 23rd of November; is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This summons was sent to you by the BH army, the defence department of Vitez. Can you recognise the signature on this summons?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think I can, because this man was the president of the fire prevention society for a time. I think his name was Sulejman, Suljo -- Kalco. Sulejman Kalco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you repeat the name?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I think his real name was Sulejman Kalco, but that he was known as Suljo Kalco.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see. Thank you. So you received summons from the BH army and from the other organisation for the same day, for the same duty. How did you explain this?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, at that time we thought, well, we are firefighters, we are not going to have problems putting out fire anywhere, wherever they occur, whether in a predominantly Muslim village or a predominantly Croatian village, that we could go to both the -- any locality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, this dual summons you understood to be the method of functioning of the community in Vitez which had begun to disintegrate in a certain way.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, and we had taken it to be normal. We knew that the two sides were engaged in a dispute, in a conflict. So we took that to be quite normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have the originals with me. I don't know whether it could be submitted as evidence or returned to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless anybody wants to keep the originals, I would have thought a copy in this case would be sufficient. The witness can return with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's move on. You were involved in the fire prevention society on a voluntary basis, but you also know at that time the village guards were being formed. Did that happen in the part of Vitez you lived in as well?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. When I went to put out fires, I would see the village guards patrolling around, and I know that they were in front of my house too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the composition of those village guards, ethnically speaking, at the beginning, and what happened as time went by?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I know that at the beginning, when they were first formed - now, what is the beginning? Well, I really don't know - but it was formed of the population, the inhabitants, living there. I suppose you mean whether they were Croats, Serbs, Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They were all together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: For what purpose were these village guards organised, according to you?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I mentioned that there were incidents that took place. There was unrest. People were afraid of the Serbs from Vlasic; Vlasic is fairly near. But it was mostly to protect one's property and family from grenades, explosions, that kind of thing. Several houses would get together, form village guards, and protect their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Were you part of the village guard system?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: For a long time I worked exclusively in fire prevention, and then the people that stood guard thought that this was a bit silly and thought that my work was less important. Because sometimes they would be on patrol all night, and they said, "Well, I think that you ought to join us, you ought to do this kind of work from time to time too." And actually that very night I stood guard, I became included in the village guards. They thought this was more serious business. So every second or third night I would spend the night patrolling the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Who organised the village guards in your area?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, the organisation itself -- I don't know that anybody actually organised it. It was sort of -- we saw this in Sarajevo on television. We saw people get together; the inhabitants of a building, for example, they would stand guard over their own property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was there a commander, somebody in charge, or a leader, somebody who imposed himself as a leader or commander?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Not at that time, although we always said, "Well, you be the head for tonight. You round up the other people." But people didn't like doing that, so they said, "Why should I? Why doesn't somebody else do that?" that kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us, Mr. Strukar, that you lived near the Mahala. At the beginning of 1993, did you see anything unusual, anything untoward in that part of town, by the football field?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, coming back from school, my son said he saw a trench there, and I said, "Well, how do you know what a trench is?" But I was interested in finding out and went past there in my own car. And I did see some sort of planks of wood and some dugouts near the Mahala. There are several Muslim houses, although people didn't really call that Mahala. But it did look like a trench, actually. So then people started saying that trenches were being dug facing the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever learn why these trenches were dug in the Mahala area?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, yes, because it was still not wartime. We were still all living together and we would talk to each other. We would talk to the Muslims and so on, and they said that it was in case of an attack from the Serbs. That was a little funny. It all seemed funny to us because, well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, I see that this makes you laugh. Why was this funny? Why does that make you laugh?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, it was strange, funny, because up until 1990 -- 1995, I never saw a Serb soldier except on television. I knew that they were up there somewhere on Mount Vlasic, behind Travnik. Travnik is 14 kilometres away from Vitez, which means that the whole thing was 25 kilometres away, at Turbe, and so on, where the army of Republika Srpska was entrenched. So two towns had to fall to reach us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, were these trenches turned towards Vlasic and Travnik, or were they facing the other part of town?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They were not towards Vlasic. It was the position towards the playing field, towards Mlakici, Kamenica, that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was the national composition living in Mlakici, where the trenches were facing?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They were Croats. Croatians lived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you like, I think it's an appropriate time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now until a few minutes after half past eleven. Mr. Strukar, we are going to take a break. Would you remember during it not to speak to anybody about your evidence until it's over and not to let anybody speak to you about it, and that does include members of the Defence team. Would you be back, please, at half past.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strukar, before we move on to address the events of the 15th and 16th of April, 1993, I should like to ask you just one more question about what happened before that. You spoke about incidents in the town, explosives planted, and so on and so forth. Are you aware of a case when an explosive was planted and property of a private entrepreneur, Nikola Krizanac, was looted. It is not far from your home. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I do, but there were two incidents, in point of fact. I don't know which of them you mean. One was before the war broke out in Vitez, and the second time, after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nikola Krizanac is a Croat, isn't he?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was the perpetrator of that identified?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: On both occasions Muslims were involved. Again, I do not know which of the incidents you are referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. Strukar, what did you do between -- during the night of the 15th, 16th April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, we at that time already had this, what we call it, village guards organised, so that I was -- so that I was awake and doing it with some of my neighbours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was that evening like any other evening before that or did anything out of the ordinary happen that evening?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't say there was anything in particular, because there had already been such evenings for the past half year or so. I don't know whether you understand it. It's men. I mean, some are not particularly brave, some are; some will make a mountain out of a molehill, others will do the opposite, so that -- but as 1993 was drawing closer, because these guards were not mixed, then there was, you know, this -- Muslims are preparing something, or I don't know. This is happening or that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned, for instance, this Nikola Krizanac shop when they blocked that road --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, you'll appreciate we've heard a lot of evidence in this case, and we'd be grateful if you would just stick to the point. As I understand it, there was nothing out of the ordinary that night, as far as you were concerned; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Nonetheless, that evening your village guards received notice by telephone; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That is what I heard, that somebody -- but that was not the first time. I have to say that somebody would just come up with a story and say, "Listen, somebody had just called to say that something was wrong, to raise the preparedness." And so that happened that evening again, but it was nothing new.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. You told us already that such communications had happened before and they did not take them too seriously; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Oh, yes, quite.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you spend that whole night on duty?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Those village guards -- I have to call them that, because everybody calls them that -- and we saw that by having, I don't know, ten of us, or five or six of us being on duty until midnight, and then others after midnight. And that night, I was assigned to the duty before the midnight, so that I had to --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So after midnight that night, you went to bed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, no, no. I went to -- I slept -- I went to bed before midnight.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And let me ask you: At the entrance and the exit from the town -- from the part of the town called Mahala, were there any checkpoints at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: You mean that evening?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: No, no, no. Not only that evening, but at about that time, in the first months of 1993 or March/April 1993.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, yes. Those checkups -- those checkpoints would be -- yes, would be erected for a couple of days and then they would come down again. Somebody would organise something and then somebody, I suppose, would talk to somebody and he would just remove that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Right. Let us go back to that evening. So you were on duty after midnight, and what did you see or hear the next morning?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We discussed this matter quite a lot, and I remember roughly we were sitting by a house, and sometime around half past 5.00, and I'm not sure whether it was five minutes before or later, but we heard an explosion from the direction of a private filling station to the left from my house, not far from the roundabout which goes around the town of Vitez. And a couple of minutes after that explosion -- we did not know, or at least I did not know what it was all about, but at that time, to my experienced ear, all the explosions sounded the same. But a couple of minutes later, rifles or pistols began firing -- I don't know -- from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Could you identify the direction from which this gunfire came and who was firing at whom?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Not then. Not at that time. And I'm only talking about my experience in war. A bullet which perhaps comes from some 10 or 15 metres, you still don't know where it comes from. It seemed to me that it was all around me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And at that time did you get any information as to what was going on?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: There was no time to seek any kind of information. All we could do was run back to one's wife and children. I was up at the time, but that doesn't mean that I knew anything more about what had happened and that I knew what was happening. There was such a disarray. It's so difficult to describe it to people in this courtroom. I mean, unless you've experienced the beginning of a war, it's difficult to say how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But at that time were you aware that the war had begun, as you put it.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, because even before, as I said, in that conflict down there, there's been some gunfire, and on a couple of occasions, and even before that. But it would all come down and one would think that it was some idiot just firing out, firing, and that it would stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But this time this fire did not die down, did it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, it did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the contrary --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: -- it began to escalate, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And as a result of this gunfire and the disarray, did it result in some perhaps fires around your house, around your building?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, after some time - I don't know how long - yes, one could see fire. But at that moment, I didn't know what was on fire. Because, I mean, you could see fire; you don't know what is on fire. Later on you simply see that houses are on fire. Since I wasn't at home at that time, I didn't know whether it was my house which was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But did you think at that moment, did it occur to you at that moment, since you were an active fireman at that time, that perhaps you should report for duty there and try to put those fires out? Was it possible at that moment?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
