I didn't see them all; I saw one or two of them, because I had my head in the sand.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did they expel the Muslims from the houses?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I didn't see that myself, but I heard during that day that they did, because the Muslims came to the houses were there were our families, and they said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: I spoke to you about weapons a minute ago. Did you or did you not see what kind of weapons those individuals had? Did they perhaps have a gun, a cannon?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: On that day or the next day or the third day, I did see a gun. I assume I probably heard it firing. It was a gun that was on a truck, and it's an anti-aircraft gun. I saw it. I didn't see it shooting. I heard it shooting at first. Later on I saw it too. It was next to the parking lot. Whether it was a day or two later that I saw it firing, I don't know. I assumed it was that gun that was firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In your earlier statement it was the first day that you saw it, not later.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I have to say again that even today it is not clear to me what happened when exactly - the first, second, third night - because I was frightened, I hadn't slept probably. Things were confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise for interrupting. I feel we are not making progress. Mr. Lopez-Terres has just told the witness that in his previous statement he said he had seen the gun on the first day. That's not what it says. It says that he heard the gun, not saw it. And that's what the witness has said today. I think that's an important difference, so I think that the question was not a fair one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Go on, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, this gun, could you please -- could you -- if you could describe it in January 1999, it is because you had seen it.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I said now that I saw it afterwards. I saw it parked by the street.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I assumed it was that gun that had fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And those young men from Nova Bila, do you know who they might be?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I have already said that we simply thought they were from Stara Bila or Nova Bila, from the direction of Travnik, because those lads were there for a brief period of time and I never saw them again afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you've been interrupted, and therefore you should have more time, but perhaps you could come to any other crucial points that you wish to make now, in about five minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did your vehicle disappear during that evening, Mr. Strukar?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Whether it was evening or morning --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And what were the circumstances under which this happened?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I learnt what my father told me. My vehicle was parked in the garage, and one of those lads who were there was wounded and they broke into my garage to take the car. They were trying to break in, so my father gave them the key, and they took the vehicle away and drove away the wounded man in my car.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you ever hear mention or rumour about a unit called Zuti?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I heard about Zuti only afterwards, during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know where that unit was stationed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know the name of Zdravko Andric?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You saw Muslims being expelled at night by those young men. You saw them moving, coming towards the place where you were; isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I saw Muslims coming, and they said that they had been expelled from their houses by those people, and their houses burnt. I didn't see that actually happening, but I saw the Muslims coming to the places where our families were, and they said that's what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And what did those Muslims look like then?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, they were like us. They were frightened. Some were dressed, others were not dressed properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was it your impression that they had just left their beds?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And why did you think those Muslims arrived to that part -- came to that part of Mahala where you were?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: They said part of Mahala -- the part where I lived is not called Mahala. They came there. I really don't know why. Perhaps there was less shooting in our area. And we were on a lower -- the ground was lower down and the bullets couldn't reach it so easily, so it was quiet. I didn't think about it much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And do you know what then befell, what happened to those Muslims after you saw them there? Did they go back to their houses?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No, they didn't go back, because all the families, the Croat and Muslim, and the Muslim men, stayed in those houses 10 or 12 days. I don't know exactly, but I know that in the end, all the food was eaten from those houses and the surrounding houses. But they stayed for at least ten days and some stayed until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And would you know if some of them were taken subsequently to detention camps?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't think they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You said this morning that you noted dead bodies.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes. When I came to my father's house, my father told me, so I looked on the road and I saw a corpse.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And that body, did it belong to a Muslim or to a Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: My father told me the name of the person. He was a Muslim, the one we could see from his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The name, would it be Sulejman Sadibasic?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you or did you not see any other bodies apart from Sulejman Sadibasic's?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: From what my father told me, there were others. He told me where they were. I don't know if you can understand this, but I had never looked at dead bodies before, and seeing just one was too much for me. I didn't wish to look. It was enough for my father to tell me they were dead, and it was enough for me to see one, to feel sick and to turn away from that sight and go back. There was simply no possibility for me to walk around looking because there were bullets still flying around.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Mr. Sulejman Sadibasic's son was also killed, and his body was lying nearby.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: As I said, I heard there were others who had been killed; my father told me. Later on I learned that his body was on the other side of the street, and I wasn't able to see it in the following five or six days.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During that night, the 15th to the 16th of April, 1993, to your knowledge, were any Croats killed?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But many houses in that neighbourhood were destroyed, weren't they? And the majority of those houses were what, Muslim or Croat?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you, if we -- I have to show it with my hands, I apologise. If this is the border of Mahala as we call it, and the other place is where the Catholic church is, on this side from the Mahala, most houses that burned were Catholic or Croat; on the other side, most of them were Muslim. So at my house, there was a kind of line, and no houses were burnt there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But you did not really reply to my question. Were there more Muslim or more Croat houses that were destroyed that night?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: More Muslim houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the morning, on the 17th of April, and the following days, did you see Darko Kraljevic not far from your house and other Croat houses in that neighbourhood?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I have thought about this a lot, and some people even told me when I testified last time that that was the day, but I simply cannot remember whether it was on the 17th, 18th, or 19th. As far as I know, about their being there, they were not on this side of the street where I was. So I didn't see them until the third, fourth, or fifth day, because they were on the other side of the street. And you simply couldn't peep out, you couldn't stick your head out, because there were bullets flying around. So we had to go round the house to go in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, I think it's about time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A last point, just one last point, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you found yourself in your house on the 18th of April, did you then hear a major explosion not far from your house?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Yes, I did. It was a big explosion. I heard it, but I wasn't at home then, I was near where my family was. And the explosion came from the direction of my house.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you know who was behind that major explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I know now, that's what I have to say. I learned some 10 or 15 days afterwards, because the Croats who stayed behind in the Mahala, when they got out of Mahala, when they were released, they told us what it had been about.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You have not answered the question. What was it about?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: It was a truck which -- as I heard, because I didn't see it myself. I have to be careful what I say now. So I was told that it was a tank truck which passed down the street and exploded.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Exploded just like that, by accident, or was it made to explode?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I wouldn't know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: But did somebody tell you that you should go to the shelter because there would be such an explosion?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: We were in shelters all the time. I remember that someone in the general chaos said something like -- that something would go off. I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This is not exactly what you said in January 1999. I can read to you the transcript, and you will tell me if you agree with what it says here: "At a given moment, into the house where I was, men entered ..." It is page 16993, "... men entered and told us to go to a shelter because there would be a major explosion." You were then asked: "Who told you that?" you did not respond, and you said that three or four minutes after that man had warned you, such a big explosion did, indeed, take place. Did you or did you not say what I have just read out to you on the 14th of January, 1999?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, another yes/no question. Well, I said the same now. We were in a shelter. Somebody came in and said that. But you're imagining it's a situation like a courtroom: Everybody else is silent and I am saying something and you are writing it down. But there were no chairs. There was chaos. It was a basement. There were mice around.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You've made the point. Thank you, Mr. Lopez-Terres. Yes, you've had an hour and a half now, and I think that really must be sufficient for cross-examination. Yes. Any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Just a few questions, Your Honour, if you please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Strukar, you have been shown Exhibit 385, that is, a BritBat report about the explosion of the bank in Vitez. In that document --

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: I apologise. When?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Today. I will put the question to you and then you will remember quite easily. This is a document written in English, composed by BritBat, and it says that in Vitez a bomb was planted in the Commercial Bank of Sarajevo. Is there such a bank in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Not now. What was before, as far as I can remember, I think it said "Privredna Banka Travnik."

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Travnik. Thank you. In that same report it says that on the following day the Zagrebacka Banka was opened in Vitez. Two questions about this: First, has there ever been a Zagrebacka Banka in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After the explosion in the bank that was called the Travnik bank, was a Zagrebacka Banka, or any other bank, ever opened?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the Chamber's reference, I would like to recall the testimony of the witness Tibold who spoke about this topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, a very brief question, although I think that you have already answered it. How many times before the night of the 15th to the 16th of April did you take your wife and children from your house to a safer place?

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: Well, I really didn't expect such questions. Do you expect us to count the times? It was some 20 times, more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's an answer. So in the night of the 15th to the 16th, it was not something exceptional, it was not for the first time.

utterances.speaker: MARIJAN STRUKAR
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Strukar, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Lopez-Terres, on reflection, having heard the cross-examination and having had the chance of seeing the witness, we shouldn't exhibit these documents. It will only confuse issues. We'll rely on the evidence. We'll hand these back. Yes. Can we have the next witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. My next witness is Mr. Dusan Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Let the witness take the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare -- I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If you'd like to take a seat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Lukovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On behalf of the Cerkez Defence, I shall be asking you a few questions. Please answer them to the best of your recollections to help us through your testimony, and please try and speak slowly to give the interpreters a chance to do their job properly. For the record, please state your name and place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Lukovic. I was born on the 22nd of September, 1935, in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, you are by nationality a Serb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You have dual citizenship of the Republic of Bosnia and the Republic of Croatia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you're an atheist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You finished the secondary teacher's training college in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: After that you graduated from the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You are married, the father of two children, and you have five grandchildren; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You're not the member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you serve the JNA, the former army?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, in 1955/1956.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you receive a rank of any kind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I received the rank of sergeant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, something about your education and what you did during the course of your working life. You graduated in 1970, I believe, from the faculty of political sciences in Sarajevo, and after that you found a job in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the Workers' University, which was called the Mosa Pijade Workers' University in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: That Workers' University was also called the Centre for Education.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the educational centre, that's right, within the composition of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What was your job?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was professor of sociology in the Centre for Education.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And how long did you work in the centre?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked there until 1972, and then I went to the secondary school centre and I was the director of the secondary school centre in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You became director, did you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you performed that function until when?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Until 1976.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And what was your job after that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: After that I joined the Slobodan Princip Seljo military factory, and I was the head of the department for legal affairs, personnel, and administration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Between 1977 and 1981 you returned.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time I was given an assignment and I went to the Workers' University, Mosa Pijade, and became the university's director.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You stayed there until 1981; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: At that time, you were also the vice-president of the Vitez municipality as a volunteer, not as a professional.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: From that year onwards, that is to say, from 1981 up until the outbreak of the conflict in Vitez, you were the director of the community for information and protection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And during that period of time, you were also president of the municipality of Vitez in two mandates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was mayor or president of the municipality from 1983/1984, that was my first mandate; and from 1984 to 1985, that was my second mandate, and the mandates lasted one year each.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Finally, you retired on the 1st of May, 1996.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: And I'm still a pensioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Yes. Thank you. At the beginning of 1992, when the war had broken out in Slovenia and Croatia with the attack of the JNA, how was this reflected on production in the SPS factory?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, at that time there was a considerable drop-off in production levels and there was serious problems with regard to raw materials, the raw materials needed to produce explosive devices. Not all the workers could stay on in the factory. The number of workers had to be cut down in line with the production decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. So at that time lots of people were without a job, or they were put on standby, is the term referred to them.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, as that category of people are not something that is common knowledge outside our country, what does it mean to be put on standby? What did that actually mean?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, as there was not enough production going on, nor enough raw materials to engage the factory at full capacity, we had to decrease our production capacities. And then the management board held a meeting to decide what to do, faced with a situation of this kind, because there was surplus labour. And they decided to send a portion of the workers home, to put them on standby, and to keep others on. And then after a month or so, to replace them, to have one group come back to work and others go back home. This would prevent tension and dissatisfaction on the part of the workers, if they took their turns.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you correctly, and please correct me if I am wrong, it was not that the workers were laid off, but they were sent home, they were put on standby, until the need for them to come back to work arose again, and then they were called up again; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Just a moment, please. There were cases where there was a technological surplus. My son was a technological surplus because he had graduated from law school and he had to go to the employment bureau. There might have been other examples of what we refer to as technological surplus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What it, in fact, meant was that your son lost his job; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and he had to go to the employment agency.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In this process, could you note any discriminatory intent with respect to the nationality of the workers?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I did not notice a single case of that. And perhaps my example will be best. I was also sent home and placed on standby because the management board decided, and I within that board, said that if workers were put on standby, then some of the managers ought to be put on standby too, that that would be fair, especially in the administrative sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, yes. And that's how you came to be placed on standby yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So you didn't -- you weren't sacked. You carried on performing your functionings but you didn't go to work regularly?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I would go to work from time to time. I would be in contact with my managers and colleagues by phone. I would go to attend meetings from time to time, and I had to go every month to sign the accounts and to determine plans for the following month, to organise the shifts and to rotate the workers, to bring those who had been put on standby back to work and to send those who had been working on standby. But in my case, they themselves made up this schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, Mr. Lukovic, the national composition of the workers in the SPS factory, did it correspond and reflect the national make-up of the municipality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I couldn't say that for certain, so perhaps I would prefer not to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In the SPS, were there more Croats compared to Muslims, or were there an equal number on both sides, or more Muslims? What would you say, on the basis of your experience?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, once again, I couldn't venture to guess. I always like to be very exact and precise. I'm sure that those facts and figures existed, but in the management of the SPS, some people said there were more Muslims than Croats; other people said other things. But these are all individual statements which are irrelevant. That is to say, it did not emanate from the policy of the management structure. The workers like to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: This brings me to my next question. The management structure, did it implement a discriminatory policy towards Muslims compared to Croats or anybody else?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the answer to that is no. Because when I was put on standby, the people who worked with me in my department, one of them was in the security department, he remained at work. Another man was the security chief, he also went to work. As far as I remember, the technical director, who was my immediate superior, he was at work too. So I did not notice that I was sent home because I was a Serb, nor that the others were sent back because they were Muslims or Croats or whatever. Now, whether we had planned everything properly and fairly, I can't say, but there was no discrimination, as far as I was able to see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes, I see. Thank you. Do you happen to know whether anybody within SPS, the factory SPS, that large conglomerate, did they ask the employed Muslims to sign any kind of loyalty oath to the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Not as far as I know, nor did anybody ask me to do so, to sign any pledge or oath of any kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukovic, on the 16th of April, 1993, there was an open-armed conflict in Vitez. Where were you on that particular morning?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: On that particular morning I was in my apartment, together with my wife and son and daughter-in-law and my two grandsons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did you do when the shooting started?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, nothing. We were all surprised. We were all afraid. We didn't know what was going on. We moved away from the windows and waited to see what would happen next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did anybody come to your building and give you any instructions?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: A man knocked at the door, and he was a member of the military police. I saw when I opened the door. And he just told us that we should go down to the basement. He said, "Go down to the basement straight away, to the cellar." And the cellars had been accommodated beforehand; that is to say, there had been two airborne attacks by the JNA when they attacked the complex, so we knew where to take shelter, in the cellars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The building you live in, how many storeys does it have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: It has a basement -- a ground floor and four floors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And the basement was used by all the tenants as a shelter in case of need?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Some of these shelters were small, so we would gather together in one of the larger shelters. Some were damp, others were not. But yes, we were downstairs in the basement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You told us that you started using the basement as a shelter in 1992, when the JNA aviation bombed Vitez.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were -- there was strong shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What happened next? From that first day onwards, what did you do? How did you behave?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I was on standby, as I said, and as they were shooting from all sides, it was dangerous to go out, and we spent most of our time indoors, in the building. You couldn't go out anywhere at that time. You did your best to take shelter and stay together with your family. So I was on complete standby. I had nothing to do, no responsibilities at all, and I didn't go to the factory at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, along with my next question, I should like to apologise, because paragraph 3 -- an error has occurred in paragraph 3.2. Instead of "the autumn," it should read "in June." So paragraph 3.2 should read "sometime in June." And we're talking about June 1993, Mr. Lukovic. Who came to your apartment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: A military policeman came to my door. He had a piece of paper in his hand, probably a list, and he read out my name, Dusan Lukovic. I said that that was indeed me. And he said that I was to report immediately to the city library, public library. And I went to the library, where I found the head of the civil defence organisation there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you went to the city library. Do you remember the man who met you there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think his name was Males.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you reported to him, did you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you then?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: He said that I was a member of the work platoon, and then he said that we were to go to dig trenches at Zabrdje, to fortify Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. So that civil defence commissioner told you that you were a member of the work platoon. Now, this fact, that you were a member of a work platoon, did you know that previously?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I never thought about wars, and I knew that I had my assignments until the age of 60. I didn't expect them to send me to a work platoon. I thought they could send me to do some other kind of work. But I accepted that stoically as my duty and responsibility, and of course this was in line with the rules and regulations, with the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: But before that day you had no wartime assignment in a work platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So he told you that you had been assigned to a work platoon and that you would have to do trench-digging at Zabrdje; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you to show where Zabrdje is on the map, but compared to Vitez, where is that?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is the south-western reaches. Vlasic is to the north, so this is at Kruscica Planina, Bobasi, Veceriska, Donja and Gornja, and Zabrdje. And there's a hunting lodge there, mountaineering lodge. It is about 1.400 metres above sea level.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: So is that a dominant feature in that part of the country?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I think it is the most dominant, and there was a settlement of weekend houses, cottages, holiday homes, and so that I knew the Zabrdje area well because I had my holiday home there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How far is Zabrdje from the city library where you were given your assignment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: By car, it is 14 kilometres, depending which road you take. If you go on foot, then it would take -- then you would walk for six or seven kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you go to that locality?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they provided a van, and the van and the driver -- his name was Vinac, his surname, but there are two brothers, Vinac, so I don't know which one of the Vinac brothers this was. But they took us to Zaselje, over Gornja Veceriska, and from there we went upwards towards Zabrdje.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many of you made up the work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm not quite sure I remember. It was in 1993, a long time ago. But I think there were between 15 and 20 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: When you arrived at that location, were you escorted, let me ask you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, they asked us -- at least, they asked me, "Dusko, do you know where Zabrdje is? Would you like an escort?" Because the terrain is not a dangerous one. And I said I didn't need an escort, because I used to walk there as a young man. I would walk there often. So I said I didn't need an escort. But they told us to report to the commander of the line at Zabrdje, and that's what we did. When we got up there, we reported to the commander of the line there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you something I asked you earlier on with respect to the SPS. What was the national composition of the work platoon you were in?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I can't give you the exact percentages, but it was a multi-ethnic work platoon. And wherever I happened to be, there were Croats, Serbs, Muslims, Romanies. We even had a Slovene amongst us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How old were these men in your work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: They were -- the younger ones were Muslims, but mostly they were elderly ones. I was the oldest man among them. There were locals who volunteered, Croats who would come from the place that my daughter-in-law came from, and her family, her relatives would come, and they were people who were 65 at the time. But they weren't duty-bound. They didn't have to go. They weren't forced to go. But I was given a work assignment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were given a work assignment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How long did you spend at Zabrdje the first time you were sent there?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I spent a day and a half there. We spent the night there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: While you were at Zabrdje and digging trenches, who was in charge of you? Who looked after you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, when we reported to the commander of the line up there, he appointed two or three soldiers who were there. Some of them went a little further off from where we were digging, but one of them was always with us, and they were armed in order to ensure our safety, to protect us. And they were young men whom we all knew.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us what unit you belonged to and who was the commander of it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you. I don't know what it was called. I don't think I could even remember all the men who were there then. Whether the unit had a name or not, I don't know. We were just told to go to Zabrdje to dig the trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The next day -- and you said you were there for a day and a half. That means you left the next day, you returned the next day. What were the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: We spent the night there, we had breakfast, and we started digging. At about 12.00 or 1.00, the soldier came by and said, "Dusko, tell your men to stop digging." I said, "Why?" He said, "Stop digging and bring all your tools with you." When I went up to him later on, he said they had been informed that they were expecting an attack, that they could expect an attack, a member of the BH army, and that they -- that we were to go home. We went home. We took up all our things.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And was there an attack? Did an attack take place?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know, but four armed members of the HVO escorted us to the village of Zaselje. They went in front of us, they had their rifles cocked, because there's a forest there. They didn't want anybody to surprise us. And we climbed down the mountain following them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you went home after that; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How much time did you spend at home before you received your second call-up?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, on the 2nd of July, our work platoon went to Zaselje. It was the beginning of July, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How were you informed that you would have to be trench-digging again?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: People came to our door, and once I received an official summons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Brought by courier?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, probably somebody sent from the civil defence department. They would say, "Go and tell Dusko to report." And our collection centre was the library. We -- our work platoon was entitled the Colony Work Platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you were sent to the Zaselje location; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: How many times did you go trench-digging?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: After Zaselje, I went to Bobasi, and then, right next to Bobasi, there was Brdjani. Then I went towards Tolovici. There's a locality called Lazine. Then we went to Barin Gaj. And later on I was mobilised by the civil defence department, and sometime in August I had a bad cold and trouble with my kidneys and bladder. I was on sick leave for a month. They thought I might have jaundice. When that month had expired, I left the locality in November. I was deployed to guard duty in Vitez, because I had lost 20 kilos in the process and they thought that it would be difficult for me to continue trench-digging and thought that I'd be better at this next job. There was a lot of construction material, and I had to ensure security and protection for the ambulances, to ensure fuel and so on. There was a mortuary there too, so that all the people who were killed and brought to the mortuary were prepared there for burial. And the burials took place at 10.00 p.m., because they did not take place during the day. So five of us were in this -- doing jobs of this kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Well, having told us all that, why do you say that funerals did not take place during the day?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, the whole of Vitez was a sort of front line. You didn't know where the shooting was coming from, it's whizzing past from all sides, so for security reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: And the parents of children who had been killed did not attend funerals. There would be civil servants who would do this. They would say their last farewell to their children and then the civil defence department would see to the funerals, and it was a difficult time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And that's where the end of the war found you, is it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, on the basis of your involvement, you enjoyed certain rights later on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you, Mr. Lukovic, to take a look at a document now and to tell us whether it is an ID you received as a member of a work platoon.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D122/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: The original to the witness and the translation -- thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Lukovic, is that the membership card that you were given when you became a member of a work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. And I have brought the originals with me, I have the originals with me. That's a photocopy. I haven't got my photograph on it because I took the photograph off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. I see. My colleague, Mr. Naumovski, has just told me that there has been a mistake in the translation of the membership card, that it was the 14th of January, 1993 instead of 1994, which it says in the original; that the number is wrong, the year.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I didn't have my glasses on. The 14th of January, 1994, that's the correct date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your assignment to the work platoon, you also gained the right to be issued certificates; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You were issued a certificate to that effect. Would you take a look at the document and tell us what it's about.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document D123/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, this is the certificate in question. It was issued on the 7th of May, 1996 by the command of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, confirming the fact that Lukovic, son of Bosko, born in 1935 -- that's you yourself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Was a member of the 92nd Viteska Regiment -- 92nd Regiment, called Viteska, from the 16th of April, 1994 to the 20th of April, 1994. I have a few questions concerning this document. First, were you ever a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment, Viteska?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I learnt this for the first time when I received this certificate. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting, Mr. Lukovic, but would you just answer my questions. Were you ever a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, never. I was a civilian in a work platoon with no uniform and no weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And you received this certificate to use it for your certificates.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and on the basis of this, I was given beneficial years of service. So when I retired, this period was counted double in my years of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, the clerks that gave you this certificate, did you tell them yourself that you were a member of the 92nd Home Guard Regiment?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never gave out any information like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, let us now move on to our final area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I think I'll need ten more minutes at the most. Could we go on?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: May I add something, please? I'd like to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, briefly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't even know that the 92nd Home Guard Regiment existed, the Viteska, and I found it funny that suddenly I seemed to be a member of it. I told my family about it. But I only learnt of that when I got this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. I have to intervene with respect to the translation again, and I thank my colleague Mr. Naumovski for pointing it out, it says in the translation that Mr. Lukovic was a member of the 92nd Viteska Regiment from the 16th to the 20th of April, 1994. It should be the 16th of April, 1993 to the 20th of April, 1994. So for one year, not four days, as this document would have it, or the translation of it, that is to say. Mr. Lukovic, you mentioned by way of introduction that your son had graduated from law school but that he had lost his job, and after that he joined up with the HVO units.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not join up with the HVO units, he was mobilised. Because he was a conscript like me, but he was younger, of course, he then became a member of the HVO in its armed component.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: He was wounded during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, at Bobasi.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: And he is an invalid, a 30-per cent invalid.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. He still has some shrapnel in his left hand and is therefore an invalid and receives invalid benefits, about 300 Deutschemarks -- to the tune of about 300 Deutschemarks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: He, too, gained the right to receive certificates; is that right? What about your wife, was she a member of any armed component of the HVO or work platoon?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, my wife was my wife. She was a housewife, a mother, and granny, and she was at home all the time. She was the backbone of our family, on duty all the time. Her husband would go off in one direction, her son in another, so she stayed at home with her daughter-in-law and her grandchildren. This was very difficult for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Yes. But she too received the certificates.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, she did, because all of us in Bosnia-Herzegovina were issued certificates from the privatisation of the socially-owned companies and factories that existed beforehand, social capital, socially-owned property. And also retired pensioners received an additional benefit, and the people who had savings accounts and lost their savings, they too were issued certificates, as did the members of the HVO, depending on the years of service in the HVO or civilian defence there. My wife, in addition to this, received about 1.000 marks' worth of certificates as a citizen who was in the area during those war days. And the women via the Red Cross did some war effort, they were engaged in a war effort. They would bake bread or pies or supply sheets for hospitals or the mortuary, things of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukovic. Yes, we get the picture. You know Mr. Mario Cerkez, do you not?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I know him very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: You know him because you knew his parents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were friends for many years. Particularly in the 1960s and 1970s we were great friends, and we would see each other socially. We would go camping together for ten years. We would go to the coast, to Makarska. So Mario and his brother Davor and their parents and my children, we would all go to the seaside together.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your friendship with the Cerkez family, could you say that the Cerkez family, and then, of course, Mario Cerkez, had any national prejudice with respect to the Muslims, or other ethnic groups living in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, the Cerkez family is a highly respected family, especially Tugomir, his late father, and Ivanka, their mother. They both worked in the post office. They were very friendly people, had many friends. Lots of people knew them. I never noticed anything of this kind, and if I did notice anything, I wouldn't be their friend. And I think it is important for me to say that both of them, particularly Mario's mother, she was a very religious lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Did you ever happen to notice that Mario was prone to aggressive behaviour of any kind, or entered into conflicts, arguments, anything of that kind?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: It's difficult -- I will give you an answer, but as I say, we are friends, so it is up to you to assess how far I can be objective, because we were great friends. But my feelings towards him: Let me say that Mario was an outstanding young man, very well brought up, highly cultured. He went to the school for reserve officers in Bileca; he was a lieutenant. He worked in the post office for a time, and later on in the secretariat for national defence, and in the civil defence services in the municipality. Later on, when I moved to the Princip Seljo factory and I was a manager there, there was the total national defence sector, and I asked Mario to come over because we were having some problems with the materiel and technical equipment. We took Mario on as a technician and an officer, and he moved to work in the factory. He was a clerk for the MTS, or materiel and technical resources department.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: In your opinion, how did he acquit himself?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, he was excellent. He was very pedantic in his work. We got through the job quickly. Of course, my assessment need not mean a great deal. But there were several military inspections which came round, there was a federal inspector headed by an admiral, and a republican inspection, and they gave a very high appraisal not only for Mario but for territorial defence in that territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: Thank you for all those details, Mr. Lukovic. Thank you for testifying. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lukovic, can I ask you something to make sure I've got your evidence right: When you said you were digging trenches, you mentioned Bobasi and Lazine as places that you went to dig trenches, and you mentioned some other places. Could you remind me of what they were?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you want me to give you all of them, all the places?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You mentioned Zaselje and Zabrdje. I have those. Now, besides Bobasi and Lazine, what were the other ones?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Brdjani and Barin Gaj. I think that makes six, six localities in all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with some other of the geography, if you would. The Workers' University, or Centre for Education, we hear, is also called -- or was also called the cultural centre; was that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the Workers' University in 1959 and it worked as an autonomous institution. But a separate thing was the cultural centre of the military factory, Slobodan Princip Seljo. Afterwards the Workers' University and the cultural centre joined up, and it became one organisation which was referred to as the Workers' University, or Mosa Pijade. Mosa Pijade. They had a theatre there, a cinema --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to ask you, that's where they had the cinema; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One other thing: About the colony, that was a part of Vitez, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN LUKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Novi Vitez, the new Vitez, where apartment buildings went up, socially-owned ones, that is to say, the factory and the municipality built workers' apartments in that area, and they called it the colony when the military factory was built. As soon as a new building came into being, it was referred to as colony. But it was a very beautiful town at one time, a lot of greenery, lots of parks, a nice place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We're going to adjourn now. Could you come back tomorrow morning? Is there any cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Not from Mr. Kordic, no, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. There will be some cross-examination from the Prosecution. So would you be back, please, tomorrow morning at half past nine to continue your evidence. Don't speak to anybody until your evidence is over, please, and that includes members of the Defence team. If the legal officer could come up, please. Thank you. We'll adjourn now. Half past nine tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 21st day of September, 2000, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.13 p.m.,
